\# Interruption vs Exception

\#sisop #kernel



\---



Both are stopping the cpu from its normal state of execution. Its like an emergency call to the cpu so it always stops what was doing.



\## INTERRUPTION

* Generated by external hardware (keyboard, network cards, disks, clocks)
* Asynchronous (you dont know when is happening)
* examples:

  * Press a key on your keyboard.
  * Network packet arrives at your network interface card (NIC).
  * Hardware timer ticks, telling the OS scheduler it is time to switch processes (preemption).
  * Hard drive finishes reading a block of data.



\## Exception

* Generated by the cpu (code)
* Synchronous (you know when)
* Examples:

  * \*\*Faults\*\*: Division by zero, accessing restricted memory (segmentation fault), or requesting a page of memory not currently in RAM (page fault).
  * \*\*Traps\*\*: Intentional software requests for OS services, known as system calls (e.g., a program asking the kernel to read a file or allocate memory).
  * \*\*Aborts\*\*: Severe hardware errors detected by the CPU.



hard errors > timers > disks > network > shell > software.



Despite differences, unix treats both very similar:

* cpu pauses execution
* saves the context on trapframe
* switches from user to kernel
* looks up in the IDT (interrupt descriptor table), in memory array
* executes the handler



\### Tools

* strace: traces process syscalls.
* ltrace: traces library calls.
